tool.name: Flask
tool.tagline: Lightweight Python web framework: routing, templates and nothing you don't ask for
tool.description: Flask is a small, explicit Python web framework built on Werkzeug (WSGI, routing, request and response objects) and Jinja (templates). You start with a single file and add structure and extensions as the project grows. It is widely used for websites, internal tools and JSON APIs, and its simplicity makes it a great way to learn how web apps really work.

glossary.def: In Flask, the Python function attached to a URL with @app.route; it runs for each matching request and returns what the browser should receive.
In Flask, the link between a URL pattern (like /posts/<int:id>) and the view function that handles it, created with @app.route.
Flask's development setting (flask run --debug) that restarts the server when you save and shows an in-browser debugger on errors. Never use it on a public server.
In a Flask route, the part before the colon in <int:post_id>: it checks that piece of the URL and converts it (here to an int) before passing it to the view.
In Flask, the name of a route, by default the view function's name (or blueprint.function); url_for builds URLs from it.
Flask's request: an object you import that always holds the request currently being handled, with its URL, form fields, JSON, headers and cookies.
A dictionary-like object in Flask (from Werkzeug) where one key can hold several values, as in ?tag=a&tag=b; get() returns the first, getlist() all of them.
The Python library Flask is built on: it handles the low-level web work (reading requests, building responses, matching URLs) and supplies the dev server and debugger.
The template language Flask uses to build HTML: {{ ... }} prints a value, {% ... %} runs logic such as loops and ifs, and |filters change how values are shown.
In Jinja, a |name added after a value to change how it is shown, such as {{ name|title }} or {{ items|length }}.
Writing a page layout once in a base template with named blocks, then having each page extend it and fill only the blocks it changes.
Automatically turning characters like < and & in a value into harmless codes before it goes into a page, so text a user typed is shown as text and never runs as code.
In Flask, a function marked with @app.context_processor whose returned dict is added to every template, so common values don't have to be passed each time.
The programming language that web browsers run, used to make pages interactive.
In Flask, a dict-like object for remembering one visitor between requests (who is logged in, a cart). By default Flask stores it inside a signed cookie in the visitor's browser.
A long random setting Flask uses to sign the session cookie and other data, so changes made by visitors are detected. Anyone who knows it can forge sessions.

A cookie with a check value computed from its contents and a secret key; if anyone changes the contents, the check no longer matches and the server rejects it. Signed is not the same as hidden: the contents stay readable.
In Flask, a short one-time notice ("Saved!") stored in the session by flash() and shown on the next page with get_flashed_messages().
A Flask extension that adds form classes with validation rules (from the WTForms library) and CSRF protection.
The dictionary on a Flask app that holds all its settings, both Flask's own (like SECRET_KEY) and yours.
A folder next to a Flask app for files that belong to one machine and must not be committed, such as a local config file or SQLite database.
In Flask, a group of related routes, templates and error handlers (say, everything for the blog) that is defined separately and then attached to the app, often under a URL prefix.
A function, usually create_app(), that builds, configures and returns a new Flask app each time it is called, instead of one global app object.
A separate package that adds a feature to Flask, such as Flask-SQLAlchemy for databases or Flask-WTF for forms; usually set up with ext.init_app(app).
When module A imports module B while B also imports A, so one of them runs before the other is finished and names are missing, causing ImportError.
A Flask object that always points at the app handling the current request (or CLI command), so code can reach its config without importing the app.
The most widely used Python library for working with SQL databases: it can build queries in Python and map tables to classes (an ORM).
In SQLAlchemy, the object that tracks the rows you load and change and sends the changes to the database in one transaction when you commit.
A Flask extension around the Alembic library that writes and applies migration files when your SQLAlchemy models change.
With an ORM such as SQLAlchemy, a Python class that describes one database table: each attribute is a column and each instance is a row.
In Flask, app.test_client(): a pretend browser that sends requests straight into your app, without a server, and returns the responses for checking.
In Flask, the state that makes current_app and g work. Flask sets it up for each request and CLI command; elsewhere you create one with app.app_context().
In Flask, the state that makes request and session work; it exists only while a request is being handled (or inside test_request_context()).
In Flask, a scratch object for storing things during one request, such as the current user or an open database connection; it is emptied when the request ends.
In Flask, a function registered with a decorator such as @app.before_request or @app.after_request so it runs at a fixed point around every request.
The standard way a Python web app and a web server talk to each other: the server calls the app once per request and gets the response back. Flask, Django and Gunicorn all speak it.
A wrapper around a whole WSGI app that sees every request before the app does (and every response after), such as Werkzeug's ProxyFix.
In Flask, a stand-in object such as request or current_app that passes everything on to the real object for the current context. (On a network, a proxy is a server that passes requests along.)
A Flask base class for class-based views: each HTTP method (get, post, delete...) is a method of the class, and Flask allows only the methods you define.
A response header telling browsers to use only the encrypted https:// version of a site for a set time, even if someone types http://.
A response header listing where a page may load scripts, styles and images from, so the browser refuses anything an attacker sneaked in.
A widely used production server for Python web apps that speak WSGI; it runs several copies (workers) of your app to handle requests in parallel.
Werkzeug middleware that makes Flask trust the X-Forwarded-* headers set by a proxy in front of it, so it sees the visitor's real address and https.
Werkzeug's stand-in object behind Flask's request, session, g and current_app: on every use it looks up the real object for the current context.
A very lightweight thread managed by a Python library (used by gevent) rather than the operating system; thousands can wait on the network at once.
The async successor of WSGI: a standard that lets Python web apps use async code and hold long connections such as WebSockets. Quart, Starlette and FastAPI use it.
A Python web framework with almost the same API as Flask, but built on ASGI so views are async and WebSockets are supported.

concepts.name: Your first Flask app
concepts.summary: Create a Flask app, attach a Python function to a URL with `@app.route`, and run it on your own computer with the development server.
concepts.why: Everything in Flask hangs off the app object, and the development server is how you see each change as you make it.
concepts.body:
When you open a **web page**, your **browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) sends a **request** to a server: a message saying "please give me the page at this address". The address is the page's **URL**, such as `http://example.com/about`. A program on the server builds the answer, the **response**, and sends it back. For a page it is usually **HTML**: text with markers like `

Title

` that tell the browser how to draw headings, paragraphs and links. The rules browsers and servers follow for this exchange are called **HTTP**. Flask is a **web framework** for Python: a small library for writing that server program. You write ordinary functions, called **views**, that return what the browser should receive, and attach each one to a URL path with the `@app.route` decorator. The app itself is an instance of `Flask`; you pass it `__name__` so Flask knows which folder your code is in and can find your other files from there. Install it into a virtual environment with `pip install flask`, save the code as `app.py` and run: ```bash flask --app app run --debug ``` If the file is called `app.py` or `wsgi.py`, plain `flask run` finds it on its own. Open `http://127.0.0.1:5000` in your browser: `127.0.0.1` means "this computer", and 5000 is the **port**, a numbered door the server listens at. `flask run` starts a **development server**: a small web server meant only for your own computer while you build. A **web server** is any program that waits for requests and sends back responses. The live copy of a site that real users rely on is called **production**; there Flask runs under a sturdier server such as Gunicorn (covered in a later lesson). `--debug` turns on **debug mode**. It restarts the server whenever you save a file, and when a view raises an exception it shows the error's stack trace in the browser with a Python console you can type into: an in-browser **debugger**. Never use debug mode on a machine others can reach over the internet: that console runs any Python code anyone types. Returning a string sends it as an HTML page. Every response also carries a three-digit **status code** saying how it went: 200 means OK, 404 means "not found". A string is fine for a quick experiment, but anything a visitor typed that you paste into it is sent as-is, so they could slip in their own HTML. Real pages use templates (a later lesson), which make that safe. The examples in these lessons use `app.test_client()`, which sends requests straight to your app inside the same Python program, with no server or browser. It's handy for trying things out.
concepts.code:
from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route("/") def index(): return "

Hello, Flask!

" @app.route("/about") def about(): return "A tiny site." # In a terminal you would run: flask --app app run --debug # Here we call the app in-process instead: client = app.test_client() r = client.get("/") print(r.status_code, r.text) # 200

Hello, Flask!

print(client.get("/missing").status_code) # 404
takeaways: app = Flask(__name__) creates the application
@app.route(path) attaches a URL to a view function
flask --app app run --debug restarts on save and shows errors in the browser
The development server and debug mode are never for production
pitfalls: Leaving --debug on for a site on the internet, which lets anyone run Python code on your server.

quiz.q: Why must debug mode never be used on a public server?
options: The interactive debugger lets anyone run Python code on the server
quiz.explain: The in-browser debugger gives a Python console, so anyone who can reach the page can run any code on the server.

concepts.name: Routes, URL variables and methods
concepts.summary: Capture parts of the URL with converters like <int:id>, choose which HTTP methods a route accepts, and understand the trailing-slash rules.
concepts.why: Clean, predictable URLs are the public face of a web app.
concepts.body:
A **route** links a URL pattern to a view. Routes can contain **variables** in angle brackets; the matching part of the URL is passed to your view as a keyword argument:

```python
@app.route("/users/<username>")
def profile(username): ...
```

A **converter** checks and converts the value: `<int:post_id>`, `<float:x>`, `<path:subpath>` (accepts slashes), `<uuid:id>`, and the default `string`, which accepts anything without a slash. If the URL doesn't fit, for example `/posts/abc` for an `int`, Flask answers 404 without calling your function.

Every request carries an **HTTP method**, a word saying what it wants. `GET` means "show me something" (clicking a link). `POST` means "here is data to handle" (submitting a form). `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` mean replace, change and delete, mostly used by programs rather than browsers.

By default a route answers only `GET` (plus `HEAD` and `OPTIONS`, two technical methods Flask handles for you). Allow others with `methods=["GET", "POST"]` and check `request.method` inside the view, or use the shortcuts `@app.get`, `@app.post`, `@app.put`, `@app.patch` and `@app.delete`, one view per method. A request with a method the route doesn't allow gets 405 Method Not Allowed.

Trailing slashes work like folders and files on your computer:

- `/projects/` (with slash) is like a folder: visiting `/projects` sends the browser on to `/projects/`, which is called a **redirect**.
- `/about` (without slash) is like a file: `/about/` is a 404.

This gives each page exactly one URL, which search engines like. Pick one style and stick to it.

Each route also has a name, its **endpoint**: by default the view function's name. You build links from endpoint names, not paths, with `url_for` (a later lesson), so two views can't share a function name.
takeaways: <converter:name> captures and converts URL parts; a mismatch is a 404
Use methods=[...] or @app.get/@app.post to choose HTTP methods
A route ending in / redirects the slashless URL; the reverse is a 404
pitfalls: Defining two views with the same function name, which gives two routes the same endpoint and fails at startup.

quiz.q: A route is defined as @app.get("/items/<int:item_id>"). What does GET /items/x return?
options: The view is called with item_id="x"
quiz.explain: The int converter doesn't match "x", so no route matches the URL and Flask answers 404.

concepts.name: Reading the request
concepts.summary: Use Flask's request object to read URL parameters, form fields, JSON data, headers, cookies and uploaded files.
concepts.why: Every interactive feature starts with reading what the browser or program sent, safely and from the right place.
concepts.body:
Inside a view, `from flask import request` gives you the request being handled right now. It looks like a global variable, but Flask makes it always refer to the current request (how is an expert topic).

A request can carry data in several places:

- `request.args`: the **query string**, the part of the URL after `?`, as in `/search?q=flask&page=2`
- `request.form`: the fields of an **HTML form** (the text boxes and buttons on a web page) sent with POST
- `request.get_json()`: **JSON** data the client sent, already **parsed** (turned from text into Python dicts and lists)
- `request.files`: uploaded files, as `FileStorage` objects with `.filename` and `.save()`
- `request.headers`, `request.cookies`, `request.method`, `request.path`

Form fields and JSON travel in the **request body**, the main content after the request's first lines. **Headers** are extra `Name: value` lines sent with every request, such as which browser is asking. **Cookies** are small values a site asked the browser to store and send back each time.

`args` and `form` are **MultiDicts**: a key may appear more than once (`?tag=a&tag=b`). `request.args.get("tag")` returns the first value, `getlist("tag")` all of them.

Use `.get()` with a default and a `type` instead of square brackets: `request.args.get("page", 1, type=int)` returns 1 for a missing or non-numeric value. A missing key with brackets, `request.form["email"]`, raises `KeyError`, which Flask turns into **400 Bad Request**. That's fine for required fields, but `.get()` lets you write your own message.

For JSON, `request.get_json()` answers 415 Unsupported Media Type if the request's `Content-Type` header doesn't say `application/json`, and 400 if the body isn't valid JSON. `get_json(silent=True)` returns `None` instead.

Treat all of this as **untrusted input**: anyone can send anything. Checking that data has the right shape before using it is **validation**; for anything beyond a field or two, use a library such as Pydantic or WTForms. Never trust `file.filename` either: pass it through `werkzeug.utils.secure_filename` before saving, so a name like `../../app.py` can't overwrite your files.
takeaways: request.args = query string, request.form = form fields, get_json() = JSON body
Use .get(key, default, type=int) and .getlist() on MultiDicts
A missing key via [] becomes a 400 Bad Request
pitfalls: Looking for POSTed form fields in request.args, or JSON in request.form.

quiz.q: A form is submitted with method="post". Where are its fields?
quiz.explain: Form fields sent with POST are parsed into request.form; request.args only holds the query string.

concepts.name: Responses, status codes and JSON
concepts.summary: Return strings, dicts, tuples or Response objects to control a response's body, status code, headers and content type.
concepts.why: Browsers and other programs that call your app both rely on the right status codes and headers, not just the body.
concepts.body:
Flask converts whatever a view returns into a `Response` object: - a **string** becomes an HTML response with status 200 - a **dict or list** is converted to JSON text (**serialized**) and sent with the header `Content-Type: application/json` - a **tuple** adds details: `(body, status)`, `(body, headers)` or `(body, status, headers)` - a **Response** object is sent as it is So `return {"error": "not found"}, 404` is a complete JSON error response. Apps that answer other programs with JSON like this, rather than pages for people, are called **APIs**. The `Content-Type` header tells the receiver what kind of data the body holds: `text/html`, `application/json`, `image/png`. These labels are called **MIME types**. `jsonify(...)` builds a JSON response explicitly and is still handy for values returned from helper functions. Flask's JSON conversion handles `datetime` (as a date string in the format HTTP uses), `UUID`, dataclasses and `Decimal`; other types must be converted first, or you teach Flask about them with a custom JSON provider. To change the response before sending it, for example to set a cookie, create it with `make_response(...)`: ```python resp = make_response("

Home

") resp.set_cookie("theme", "dark", httponly=True) ``` `httponly=True` hides the cookie from JavaScript running in the page, a good default. `redirect(url)` answers with status 302, which sends the browser to `url`. Use `code=303` after a POST, and `301` or `308` when a page has moved for good. For files, `send_file` and `send_from_directory` send a file from disk piece by piece with the right headers. `send_from_directory` refuses paths that lead outside the folder you name, so use it whenever the file name comes from untrusted input. Use status codes deliberately: 201 Created for something new, 204 No Content for success with nothing to send back, 400 for bad input, 404 for missing, 409 for a conflict (such as a username already taken).
takeaways: str -> HTML, dict/list -> JSON, a tuple adds status and headers
make_response() when you need to set cookies or headers on the response
redirect() defaults to 302; choose status codes deliberately
pitfalls: Returning status 200 with an error message in the body instead of a proper 4xx status.

quiz.q: What does return {"ok": False}, 400 produce?
options: A 500 error because tuples aren't allowed
quiz.explain: A dict is converted to JSON and the second tuple item sets the status code.

concepts.name: Rendering Jinja templates
concepts.summary: Build HTML pages from files in templates/ with render_template, pass in values, and rely on autoescaping and template inheritance.
concepts.why: Real pages need layouts, loops and safe handling of user text, which hand-built strings get wrong.
concepts.body:
Building HTML by gluing strings together gets messy and unsafe fast. Instead, Flask keeps each page in a **template**: an HTML file with placeholders that are filled with data on every request. Producing the finished page is called **rendering**.

Flask's template language is **Jinja**. Put templates in a `templates/` folder next to your app module and call `render_template("page.html", **variables)`.

Inside a template:

- `{{ expression }}` outputs a value; `{{ user.name }}` works for attributes and dict keys
- `{% if %}`, `{% for %}` and `{% endfor %}` provide logic
- `{{ value|filter }}` changes how a value is shown, such as `|title`, `|length` or `|default("none")`; these are **filters**

**Autoescaping** is on for `.html`, `.htm`, `.xml`, `.xhtml` and `.svg` templates: characters like `<` in a value are turned into harmless codes (`<`), so `<script>` in a user's name is shown as text instead of running as code. That blocks **XSS** (cross-site scripting), where an attacker gets their JavaScript, the language browsers run, into pages other people view. Only mark content safe (`|safe` or `Markup`) when you generated it yourself and trust it completely.

Layouts use **template inheritance**. A `base.html` holds the page skeleton with named blocks; each page starts with `{% extends "base.html" %}` and fills blocks like `{% block content %}`.

A few objects are available in every template without passing them: `request`, `session`, `g`, `config`, `url_for()` and `get_flashed_messages()` (each has its own lesson). You can add your own with a **context processor**: a function marked `@app.context_processor` that returns a dict.

For quick experiments, `render_template_string` renders a template from a string, with autoescaping always on. In real apps prefer files: Flask keeps them loaded after first use, and editors highlight them.

Keep logic in views and presentation in templates. If a template needs complex computation, prepare the data in Python first.
concepts.code:
from flask import Flask, render_template_string app = Flask(__name__) # In a real app this lives in templates/users.html and you call render_template. PAGE = """

{{ title|title }}

    {% for u in users %}
  • {{ u.name }}{% if u.admin %} (admin){% endif %}
    • {% endfor %}

{{ users|length }} users, path {{ request.path }}

""" @app.get("/users") def users(): data = [{"name": "Ann", "admin": True}, {"name": "", "admin": False}] return render_template_string(PAGE, title="team members", users=data) print(app.test_client().get("/users").text) #

Team Members

#
  • Ann (admin)
  • <script>x</script>
#

2 users, path /users
takeaways: render_template("x.html", **vars) renders templates/x.html
{{ }} outputs values, {% %} runs logic, |filters change how values look
Autoescaping protects .html templates from XSS; |safe turns it off
pitfalls: Using |safe on user-provided content, which reopens the XSS hole autoescaping closed.

quiz.q: A user's name is Bo. What does {{ name }} render in an .html template?
options: The text Bo, with the tags escaped so they show literally
quiz.explain: Autoescaping turns < and > into harmless codes, so the tags display as text instead of making Bo bold.

concepts.name: url_for, redirects and static files
concepts.summary: Build URLs from endpoint names with url_for, redirect between views, and serve CSS, JavaScript and images from static/.
concepts.why: Hand-typed URLs break when routes change; url_for keeps every link correct.
concepts.body:
`url_for(endpoint, **values)` builds a URL from an endpoint name (the view function's name by default) and its route variables:

```python
url_for("show_post", post_id=7)        # '/posts/7'
url_for("search", q="flask", page=2)   # '/search?q=flask&page=2'
```

Arguments that aren't route variables go into the **query string**, the part after `?`. Characters that can't appear in a URL, such as spaces, are replaced by `%` codes for you (a space becomes `%20`). Pass `_external=True` for a full URL including `http://` and the site's name, which you need in emails.

Why bother instead of typing `"/posts/7"`? You can change a route's path in one place, and every link and redirect follows. A misspelled endpoint fails loudly with `BuildError` instead of producing a broken link.

`url_for` needs to know which app it is working for, so call it inside a view, a template, or a `with app.test_request_context():` block (which pretends a request is in progress, as in the code).

Some files are sent to the browser exactly as they are on disk: **CSS** (the style rules for colours and layout), JavaScript and images. These are **static files**. Put them in a `static/` folder; the development server sends them at `/static/...` under the endpoint `static`:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='css/site.css') }}">
```

In production, let a dedicated web server such as Nginx, or a **CDN** (a network of servers around the world that keep copies of your files close to users), send them directly. That is much faster than going through Python.

Combine `redirect` with `url_for` to send the browser elsewhere: `return redirect(url_for("login"))`. After a form submitted with POST succeeds, always redirect to a normal page. Otherwise refreshing the page makes the browser send the form again. This habit is called Post/Redirect/Get.
takeaways: url_for(endpoint, **values) builds URLs; extra values become the query string
Static files live in static/ and are linked with url_for('static', filename=...)
Redirect after a successful POST (Post/Redirect/Get)
pitfalls: Typing paths by hand in templates, which silently break when a route changes.

quiz.q: Given @app.get("/u/<name>") def profile(name), what does url_for("profile", name="ann", tab="posts") return?
quiz.explain: name fills the route variable, and the extra argument tab becomes a query-string parameter.

concepts.name: abort and error handlers
concepts.summary: Stop a request early with abort(404), and send custom pages or JSON for errors with @app.errorhandler.
concepts.why: People and programs using your app deserve clear, consistent errors instead of default pages or stack traces.
concepts.body:
`abort(status)` raises an `HTTPException`, which immediately ends the request with that status code. Use it for early exits at the top of a view: `abort(404)` when a record doesn't exist, `abort(403)` when the user isn't allowed. You can add a message: `abort(400, description="missing email")`.

Without your own handlers, Flask sends plain HTML error pages built by **Werkzeug**, the library Flask is built on. Register your own with `@app.errorhandler`, keyed by status code or exception class:

```python
@app.errorhandler(404)
def not_found(e):
    return render_template("404.html"), 404
```

Return the status code explicitly; otherwise the handler's response goes out as a 200.

For a JSON API, one handler for `HTTPException` covers every HTTP error: read `e.code`, `e.name` and `e.description` and return them as JSON.

An exception your code doesn't catch becomes **500 Internal Server Error**. In debug mode you see the error's stack trace; in production the user sees the 500 page (customise it with `@app.errorhandler(500)`) and the error is written to the app's log, `app.logger`, so you can find it later. You can also register handlers for your own exception classes, such as a `NotFoundError` raised deep inside your code, and turn them into HTTP responses in one place.

Handlers registered on the app apply everywhere. Blueprints (a later lesson: groups of routes) can register their own, which win for errors raised inside the blueprint's views. But 404 and 405 happen before any view is chosen, so only app-level handlers see them.
takeaways: abort(code) ends a request immediately with an HTTP error
@app.errorhandler(code or exception class) customises the response
Handlers must return the status code themselves
pitfalls: Forgetting the status in an error handler, so the custom 404 page is sent as 200.

quiz.q: An error handler for 404 returns only render_template("404.html"). What status does the client get?
quiz.explain: The handler's return value is a normal response; without an explicit code it is 200.

concepts.name: Sessions and cookies
concepts.summary: Remember each visitor between requests with Flask's session, stored in a signed cookie and protected by a strong SECRET_KEY.
concepts.why: Logins, shopping carts and one-time messages all depend on remembering the visitor from one request to the next.
concepts.body:
Each HTTP request arrives on its own: the server keeps no memory of earlier ones, which is why HTTP is called **stateless**. To remember a visitor, Flask gives you `session`, a dict-like object it saves between requests.

By default Flask stores the session inside a cookie in the visitor's browser. The dict is turned into text (**serialized**) and **signed** with your `SECRET_KEY`: a check value is added that only someone who knows the key can compute, so a visitor who edits the cookie gets it rejected. This is a **signed cookie**.

Signed is not hidden. The cookie is not **encrypted** (scrambled so only key holders can read it); it is merely written in base64, a text encoding anyone can undo. Never store passwords or secrets in it; store an identifier like `user_id`.

`SECRET_KEY` must be long and random, for example from `python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex())"`, and loaded from configuration rather than written in code (see the Configuration lesson). If the key leaks, attackers can forge sessions and log in as anyone. Flask 3.1 adds `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS`, a list of old keys still accepted for reading, so you can switch to a new key without signing everybody out.

Behaviour to know:

- Sessions end when the browser closes, unless you set `session.permanent = True`; then `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` (31 days by default) applies.
- Flask notices assignment (`session["cart"] = ...`) but not changes inside a nested value. After `session["cart"].append(x)`, set `session.modified = True`.
- Cookies are limited to about 4 KB, so keep sessions small.
- Call `session.clear()` on log-out.

Cookie settings matter. `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY` is on by default (JavaScript in the page can't read the cookie). In production also set `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True`, so the cookie is only sent over **HTTPS** (encrypted HTTP), and `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = "Lax"`, so other websites can't make the browser send it along with their requests.

For large sessions, or ones you must be able to cancel from the server, extensions such as Flask-Session keep the data in a database or in Redis (a fast in-memory store) and put only an ID in the cookie.
takeaways: session is a signed (not encrypted) cookie: readable, but not forgeable
Use a long random SECRET_KEY loaded from configuration
Set session.modified = True after changing nested values
pitfalls: Storing sensitive data in the session, assuming it is encrypted.

quiz.q: A user decodes their Flask session cookie. What can they do?
options: Read its contents, but not change them without breaking the signature
quiz.explain: The default session is signed, not encrypted: the visitor can read it, but any change breaks the signature.

concepts.name: Handling forms with Post/Redirect/Get
concepts.summary: Handle HTML form submissions: check the fields, show the form again with errors, and flash a message and redirect on success.
concepts.why: Forms are how users change data, and redirecting after success avoids duplicate submissions.
concepts.body:
A typical form view answers two methods: `GET` shows the empty form, `POST` handles what was submitted.

The flow for a POST:

1. Read fields from `request.form` with `.get()` and strip spaces.
2. Validate. If there are errors, **render the form again** with the error messages and what the user typed, and return status 400 or 422 ("unprocessable") so tests and tools see the failure.
3. On success, save, `flash()` a confirmation and **redirect** to another page.

That last redirect is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern. Without it, refreshing the result page makes the browser send the POST again, and you get duplicate orders.

`flash(message, category)` stores a short one-time notice in the session for the next request; the template shows it with `get_flashed_messages(with_categories=True)`. These **flash messages** need `SECRET_KEY`, because they live in the session.

Hand-written validation is fine for two fields. For real forms most projects use **Flask-WTF**, which brings form classes with validation rules from the WTForms library and draws the fields for you.

Flask-WTF also adds **CSRF** protection. CSRF (cross-site request forgery) is an attack where another website quietly makes a logged-in visitor's browser submit your form. The defence is a hidden random value, a **CSRF token**, placed in your own form and checked on every POST; another site can't know it. Flask itself has no CSRF protection, so a plain form like the example is open to this attack in production.

For file uploads, set `enctype="multipart/form-data"` on the `<form>` tag, read `request.files["photo"]`, and cap upload size with `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`.
takeaways: GET shows the form; POST validates and either shows it again or redirects
Redirect after success so refreshing doesn't resubmit
flash() needs SECRET_KEY; Flask-WTF adds validation and CSRF tokens
pitfalls: Shipping HTML forms without CSRF protection; Flask doesn't add it for you.

quiz.q: Why redirect after successfully handling a form POST?
options: So reloading the page doesn't resubmit the POST
Flask requires it for flash() to work
quiz.explain: After a redirect the browser's current page is a GET, so a refresh repeats the harmless GET.

concepts.name: Configuration and secrets
concepts.summary: Load settings into app.config from classes, files and FLASK_-prefixed environment variables, keeping secrets out of your code.
concepts.why: The same code must run on your laptop, in tests and in production with different settings, and without secrets in version control.
concepts.body:
`app.config` is a dict holding Flask's own settings (`SECRET_KEY`, `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`...) and yours. The helper methods below only load **UPPERCASE** names, which is how they skip other attributes of a class or module.

Ways to fill it, usually combined in this order so later sources override earlier ones:

- `app.config.from_object("myapp.config.Default")`: defaults from a class or module
- `app.config.from_file("config.toml", load=tomllib.load, text=False)` or `from_pyfile("instance.cfg", silent=True)`: a **config file** for one machine or server (TOML is a simple `name = value` format)
- `app.config.from_prefixed_env()`: every `FLASK_*` environment variable, with the prefix removed
- `app.config.update(...)`, or `create_app(test_config)` (a later lesson), for tests

An **environment variable** is a named value the operating system hands to a program when it starts, outside the code: `FLASK_ITEMS_PER_PAGE=50 flask run`. `from_prefixed_env()` reads the value as JSON when it can, so `FLASK_MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH=1048576` becomes an int and `FLASK_DEBUG=true` a bool. A double underscore sets nested keys: `FLASK_DB__HOST`.

The **instance folder** (`app.instance_path`, next to your package) is for files that belong to one machine and must not be committed, such as a local config file or SQLite database. Create the app with `instance_relative_config=True` to load files relative to it.

A **secret** is anything like `SECRET_KEY`, a database password or an **API key** (a password your code uses to call another service) that must not leak. Keep secrets in environment variables or a **secrets manager** (a service that stores them and hands them only to your app), never in source code. Check required settings at startup and fail at once: a missing `SECRET_KEY` should stop the app from starting, not show up as a confusing error at the first log-in.

In code, read settings with `current_app.config["KEY"]` (`current_app` is the app handling the current request) rather than importing the app object.
concepts.code:
import os
from flask import Flask

class Default:
    APP_NAME = "Notes"
    MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 1024 * 1024
    ITEMS_PER_PAGE = 20
    lowercase_is_ignored = True

os.environ.update({"FLASK_SECRET_KEY": "from-env", "FLASK_ITEMS_PER_PAGE": "50",
                   "FLASK_FEATURES__BETA": "true"})

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config.from_object(Default)
app.config.from_prefixed_env()
if not app.config.get("SECRET_KEY"):
    raise RuntimeError("SECRET_KEY must be set")

print(app.config["ITEMS_PER_PAGE"], type(app.config["ITEMS_PER_PAGE"]).__name__)  # 50 int
print(app.config["FEATURES"])                     # {'BETA': True}
print("lowercase_is_ignored" in app.config)       # False
print(app.config["SECRET_KEY"])                   # from-env
takeaways: from_object for defaults, from_file/from_pyfile per machine, from_prefixed_env for FLASK_* variables
Only UPPERCASE names are loaded
Secrets come from the environment; fail at startup when they are missing
pitfalls: Committing SECRET_KEY or database passwords to version control.

quiz.q: With app.config.from_prefixed_env(), what does FLASK_PAGE_SIZE=25 set?
quiz.explain: The FLASK_ prefix is removed and the value is read as JSON when possible, so 25 becomes an int.

concepts.name: Organizing with blueprints
concepts.summary: Group related routes, templates and error handlers into blueprints with URL prefixes, and build their URLs with dotted endpoints.
concepts.why: A single app.py doesn't stay readable as an app grows; blueprints are how Flask splits it into parts.
concepts.body:
Once an app has dozens of routes, one file gets unwieldy. A **blueprint** is a group of routes (and templates, error handlers...) defined on its own and attached to the app later. It lets you split an application by feature: `auth`, `blog`, `api`.

```python
bp = Blueprint("blog", __name__, url_prefix="/blog")

@bp.get("/")
def index(): ...
```

Attach it with `app.register_blueprint(bp)`. The `url_prefix` is put in front of every route, and endpoint names get the blueprint's name in front, a **namespace** that keeps them apart: `url_for("blog.index")`. Inside the same blueprint, the short form `url_for(".index")` refers to its own endpoint.

A blueprint can have its own:

- `template_folder` and `static_folder`
- `@bp.errorhandler`, which applies to errors raised in its views
- `@bp.before_request`, a function run before each of its routes (`@bp.before_app_request` runs before every request of the app); a later lesson covers these hooks
- `@bp.app_template_filter` and context processors

A blueprint can be registered more than once with different `url_prefix` or `name` values, and blueprints can be nested with `parent.register_blueprint(child)`. That is handy for versioned APIs, where `/api/v1` and `/api/v2` live side by side.

A common layout puts each blueprint in its own module inside a package (`myapp/auth.py`, `myapp/blog.py`) and registers them all in one place, the application factory (next lesson). Blueprints never import the app object. If they did, the app module would import the blueprint and the blueprint the app, a **circular import** that fails with `ImportError`. When a blueprint needs the app, it uses `current_app`, which always points at the app handling the current request.

Templates from all blueprints share one search list, so give each its own subfolder: `templates/blog/index.html`, rendered as `"blog/index.html"`.
takeaways: Blueprint(name, __name__, url_prefix=...) groups related routes
Endpoints become name.view; url_for(".view") stays inside the blueprint
Blueprints use current_app instead of importing the app, avoiding circular imports
pitfalls: Putting blueprint templates directly in templates/ so names collide across blueprints.

quiz.q: A view index is registered on Blueprint("admin", __name__). How do you build its URL from another blueprint?
quiz.explain: Blueprint endpoints get the blueprint name in front; the leading-dot form only works inside the same blueprint.

concepts.name: The application factory
concepts.summary: Create the app inside a create_app() function that loads config, initializes extensions and registers blueprints.
concepts.why: A factory lets tests and different environments build fresh, differently configured apps, with nothing happening just because a module was imported.
concepts.body:
Instead of a global `app = Flask(__name__)`, larger projects build the app inside a function, the **application factory**:

```python
def create_app(test_config=None):
    app = Flask(__name__, instance_relative_config=True)
    ...
    return app
```

Benefits:

- **Testing**: each test can create an app with its own settings, such as a temporary database.
- **Several environments**: your laptop, a staging copy for final checks, and production differ only in the settings passed in or loaded.
- **No circular imports**: modules never import a global app. Blueprints are registered inside the factory, and code that needs the app uses `current_app`.

**Flask extensions** (add-on packages such as Flask-SQLAlchemy) follow the init_app pattern: create the extension object at module level without an app (`db = SQLAlchemy()`), then connect it inside the factory with `db.init_app(app)`. The extension keeps its per-app data on the app (in `app.extensions`), so one extension object can serve several apps.

The `flask` command finds a factory named `create_app` or `make_app` by itself: `flask --app myapp run` works if `myapp/__init__.py` defines one. You can also be explicit: `flask --app "myapp:create_app(debug=True)" run`. Gunicorn, the production server, accepts the same form: `gunicorn "myapp:create_app()"`.

Keep the factory boring and predictable: load config, set up extensions, register blueprints, error handlers and commands, return the app. Don't do slow work there, such as connecting to the database; connect when a request first needs it.
takeaways: create_app() builds a configured app on demand
Extensions: create without an app, then ext.init_app(app) in the factory
Use current_app instead of importing a global app
pitfalls: Importing app from the package inside blueprints, which brings back circular imports.

quiz.q: Why do extensions provide init_app(app) instead of only Extension(app)?
options: So the extension object can exist before any app and be bound inside a factory
init_app is required by Flask's server
quiz.explain: Creating the extension without an app lets modules import it, while the factory connects it to each app it creates.

concepts.name: Using a database with Flask-SQLAlchemy
concepts.summary: Define models with Flask-SQLAlchemy, query with db.select and db.session, and answer 404 for missing rows with get_or_404.
concepts.why: Most Flask apps keep their data in a SQL database, and Flask-SQLAlchemy ties database sessions to requests for you.
concepts.body:
Flask has no database layer of its own. The most common choice is **Flask-SQLAlchemy** (`pip install flask-sqlalchemy`), which plugs **SQLAlchemy**, Python's most widely used SQL library, into Flask. SQLAlchemy is an **ORM** (object-relational mapper): you describe each table as a Python class, a **model**, and work with rows as objects instead of writing SQL by hand.

- `db = SQLAlchemy(model_class=Base)`, where `Base` subclasses `DeclarativeBase`
- set `SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI` to say which database: `sqlite:///app.db` or `postgresql+psycopg://...`
- models subclass `db.Model` with typed columns: `id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)`
- queries are built in Python and run through `db.session` (explained below): `db.session.execute(db.select(User).where(User.name == "ann")).scalars().all()`, or the shorter `db.session.scalars(...)` (`scalars()` gives you the model objects themselves rather than rows)
- shortcuts for views: `db.get_or_404(User, id)`, `db.first_or_404(stmt)`, `db.paginate(stmt, per_page=20)`

`db.session` is a **database session**: the object that tracks what you load and change, and sends the changes in one transaction when you commit. Flask-SQLAlchemy gives each request its own and removes it when the request ends. You still decide when to write: `db.session.add(obj)`, then `db.session.commit()`. If something fails part-way, call `db.session.rollback()`.

`db.create_all()` creates missing tables, which is fine for prototypes and tests, but it never changes existing ones. Real projects use **Flask-Migrate** (built on the Alembic library) to generate and apply migrations.

Avoid the older `User.query.filter_by(...)` style in new code; it still works, but `db.select` is the documented approach for SQLAlchemy 2.

If you'd rather not use an ORM, Flask's own tutorial shows the built-in `sqlite3` module, with a connection kept in `g` (a per-request scratch object) and closed when the request ends.
concepts.code:
from flask import Flask
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
db = SQLAlchemy(model_class=Base)

class Note(db.Model):
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    text: Mapped[str]
app = Flask(__name__)
app.config["SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI"] = "sqlite:///:memory:"
db.init_app(app)
@app.post("/notes/<text>")
def add(text):
    note = Note(text=text)
    db.session.add(note); db.session.commit()
    return {"id": note.id}, 201
@app.get("/notes/<int:nid>")
def show(nid):
    return {"text": db.get_or_404(Note, nid).text}
with app.app_context(): db.create_all()
c = app.test_client()
print(c.post("/notes/hello").json, c.get("/notes/1").json, c.get("/notes/9").status_code)
# {'id': 1} {'text': 'hello'} 404
takeaways: Flask-SQLAlchemy gives db.Model, db.session and Flask-aware helpers
Query with `db.select(...)` and `db.session.execute(...)` / `db.session.scalars(...)`
Commit explicitly; use Flask-Migrate for schema changes
pitfalls: Relying on db.create_all() to apply schema changes to an existing database; it only creates missing tables.

quiz.q: You add a column to a model in an app with existing data. What updates the database schema?
quiz.explain: create_all only creates missing tables; altering existing tables requires a migration.

concepts.name: Testing with pytest and the test client
concepts.summary: Write pytest fixtures that build the app with test settings, then drive it with the test client and the command runner.
concepts.why: Tests let you change routes, templates and queries with confidence, and Flask runs them fast without a server.
takeaways: Build the app in a fixture with TESTING=True and test settings
client.get/post(..., data=, json=, follow_redirects=) drive the app without a server
The client keeps cookies, so log-in flows can be tested end to end
pitfalls: Sharing one app or database across tests, so tests depend on each other's leftovers.

quiz.q: What does TESTING=True change when a view raises an exception during a test request?
options: The test client retries the request
The exception propagates to the test instead of becoming a 500 response
quiz.explain: In testing mode Flask raises unhandled exceptions again, so tests show the real error.

concepts.name: Application context, request context and g
concepts.summary: Understand when current_app, request, session and g are available, and push contexts yourself outside requests.
concepts.why: "Working outside of application context" is the most common Flask error, and contexts explain it.
concepts.body:
`request`, `session` and `current_app` look like global variables, yet each request sees its own. Flask achieves this with **contexts**: bits of state it sets up around each request and tears down afterwards. During a request, Flask activates (pushes):

- the **application context**, which makes `current_app` and `g` work
- the **request context**, which makes `request` and `session` work

Both are removed (popped) when the response has been sent. Outside a request, for example in a script, a terminal command, a separate thread or the Python REPL, there is no context, and touching `current_app` raises `RuntimeError: Working outside of application context`. Push one yourself:

```python
with app.app_context():
    init_db()
```

Commands registered with `@app.cli.command()` already run inside an app context. For code that needs `request`, or `url_for` with a full site address, use `app.test_request_context("/path")`.

**`g`** is a scratch object for data that should last for one app context, which in practice means one request. It is the right place for per-request things: the current user loaded from the session, or a database connection opened the first time it's needed.

```python
def get_db():
    if "db" not in g:
        g.db = connect()
    return g.db
```

Clean up with `@app.teardown_appcontext`, which runs when the context ends, even after an exception.

Don't store anything on `g` expecting it to survive to the next request; it won't. Use the session or a database for that. And don't save `request` or `current_app` in a global variable or hand them to another thread: they are stand-ins (**proxies**) that look up the real object, and they only work while their context is active.
takeaways: During a request, current_app/g and request/session are available
Outside a request, push a context with app.app_context() or test_request_context()
g holds per-request things; clean up in teardown_appcontext
pitfalls: Expecting values on g to still be there in the next request.

quiz.q: A script calls a helper that uses current_app.config and fails with "Working outside of application context". What fixes it?
options: Calling the helper inside with app.app_context():
quiz.explain: current_app only works while an application context is pushed; outside requests you push one yourself.

concepts.name: Request hooks and middleware-like logic
concepts.summary: Run code around every request with before_request, after_request and teardown_request, and know when each one runs.
concepts.why: Login checks, timing, extra headers and clean-up belong in hooks, not copied into every view.
concepts.body:
Some code should run for every request: timing it, checking a login, adding a header. Flask lets you register **hooks**, functions run at fixed points around each request:

- `@app.before_request`: runs before the view. If it returns anything other than `None`, that becomes the response and the view is **skipped**, perfect for "redirect to log-in" or turning requests away early.
- `@app.after_request`: receives the response object and **must return** a response (usually the same one). Use it to add headers. It does **not** run if an exception went unhandled.
- `@app.teardown_request` and `@app.teardown_appcontext`: always run at the end, with the exception (or `None`) as argument. They can't change the response; use them for clean-up.

`@app.url_value_preprocessor` and `@app.url_defaults` handle a URL part shared by many routes, such as a language code in `/<lang>/...`.

Blueprints have the same hooks for their own routes (`@bp.before_request`) plus app-wide versions (`@bp.before_app_request`). Several `before_request` functions run in the order they were registered; `after_request` functions run in reverse.

For a check that only some views need, a decorator such as `login_required` wrapped around those views is often clearer than a global hook with a list of exceptions.

Hooks run inside Flask. **WSGI** is the standard interface between a Python web app and the server running it; a **WSGI middleware** wraps the whole app at that level, as in `app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(app.wsgi_app)`, and sees every request before Flask does. Use middleware for low-level fixes to the raw request (ProxyFix corrects the visitor's address when a proxy server sits in front of the app), and hooks for your app's logic.
takeaways: before_request returning a value skips the view
after_request must return the response and is skipped after unhandled errors
teardown_* always runs and is for clean-up
pitfalls: Forgetting to return the response from an after_request function.

quiz.q: A before_request function returns ("Login required", 401). What happens?
options: The 401 response is sent and the view is skipped
The view runs and its result is discarded
quiz.explain: Any value other than None from before_request is used as the response, ending the request early.

concepts.name: Class-based views and JSON APIs
concepts.summary: Use MethodView to map HTTP methods to class methods for REST-style resources, and reuse logic across views.
concepts.why: REST-style APIs repeat the same GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE structure for each kind of data, which classes express compactly.
concepts.body:
Many JSON APIs follow a style called **REST**: each kind of thing (items, users) gets its own URLs, and the HTTP method says what to do with it. `GET /items/` lists items, `POST /items/` creates one, `GET`, `PATCH` or `DELETE /items/7` reads, changes or removes item 7. Each such kind of thing is called a resource.

Function views are Flask's default, but for REST resources a **`MethodView`** maps each HTTP method to a method of a class:

```python
class ItemAPI(MethodView):
    def get(self, item_id): ...
    def patch(self, item_id): ...
    def delete(self, item_id): ...
```

Register it with `app.add_url_rule("/items/<int:item_id>", view_func=ItemAPI.as_view("item"))`; `"item"` becomes the endpoint name. Flask reads which methods the class defines and allows only those; others get 405.

A common pattern uses two URLs for one resource: a **collection** (`/items/`, with `get` to list and `post` to create) and an **item** (`/items/<id>`, with `get`, `patch`, `delete`). A small helper function can register both for any model, which is where classes shine: subclass, set `model = User`, and reuse everything.

Details:

- `as_view(name, *args)` passes extra arguments to `__init__`. Set `init_every_request = False` to create the object once instead of per request (only safe if it stores nothing about a particular request).
- `decorators = [login_required]` as a class attribute applies decorators to the generated view function.
- The plain `View` base class with a `dispatch_request` method is the lower-level alternative.

For larger APIs, extensions such as Flask-Smorest or APIFlask add validation, serialization and automatically generated API documentation (in the OpenAPI format) on top of this pattern. If an API is your main goal and you're starting fresh, also consider FastAPI.
takeaways: MethodView maps HTTP methods to class methods; the allowed methods follow from them
Register with add_url_rule(path, view_func=Cls.as_view("name"))
A collection view plus an item view together form a REST resource
pitfalls: Storing per-request data on self with init_every_request = False, which shares it between requests.

quiz.q: A MethodView defines only get and delete. What does a PUT to its URL return?
quiz.explain: The allowed methods come from the methods the class defines, so other methods get 405.

concepts.name: Security essentials
concepts.summary: Protect a Flask app against XSS, CSRF, session theft and oversized requests with escaping, tokens, cookie settings and limits.
concepts.why: Flask is minimal by design, so several protections that bigger frameworks switch on by default are your job.
concepts.body:
What Flask gives you, and what you must add:

**XSS (cross-site scripting).** Jinja autoescapes `.html` templates. The holes are `|safe` or `Markup(...)` on user input, building HTML strings in Python, attribute values without quotes, and user data placed inside `<script>`. For data handed to JavaScript, use the `|tojson` filter.

**CSRF.** Flask has **no** CSRF protection. Every form, and every API that relies on the login cookie, needs tokens on requests that change data, usually via Flask-WTF's `CSRFProtect(app)`. `SameSite` cookies add a second layer.

**Sessions and cookies.** Use a long random `SECRET_KEY` and set:

```python
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True, SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True, SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax"
```

**Size limits.** Set `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` to cap the size of request bodies; bigger requests get 413 ("too large"), so nobody can exhaust your memory with a huge upload. Flask 3.1 also has `MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE` and `MAX_FORM_PARTS` for file-upload forms.

**Host header.** Every request names the site it is for in its `Host` header, and an attacker can fake it. Set `TRUSTED_HOSTS` (Flask 3.1), or check it at the server in front of Flask, so links built with `_external=True`, such as password-reset emails, can't point to the attacker's site.

**Security headers.** Add **HSTS** (always use HTTPS for this site), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (don't guess file types), `X-Frame-Options` (don't show this page inside another site's frame) or a **Content Security Policy** (only load scripts from these places). Set them in `after_request`, at the server in front of Flask, or with an extension such as Flask-Talisman.

**Passwords.** Store only a hash, a scrambled fingerprint that can be checked but not reversed: `werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash` (using the scrypt method by default), checked with `check_password_hash`. Never store or log plain passwords.

**Files.** Always run user-supplied file names through `secure_filename` and send user files with `send_from_directory`.

Finally, never run a public site in debug mode, and keep your packages updated.
concepts.code:
from flask import Flask, request
from werkzeug.security import check_password_hash, generate_password_hash
from werkzeug.utils import secure_filename

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config.update(
    SECRET_KEY="load-me-from-the-environment",
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True,
    SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax",
    MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH=1024,              # bytes
)

@app.after_request
def security_headers(resp):
    resp.headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff"
    resp.headers["X-Frame-Options"] = "DENY"
    return resp

@app.post("/upload")
def upload():
    return {"bytes": len(request.get_data())}
print(app.test_client().post("/upload", data="x" * 5000).status_code)   # 413
h = generate_password_hash("hunter2")
print(h.split(":")[0], check_password_hash(h, "hunter2"))   # scrypt True
print(secure_filename("../../etc/passwd"))                  # etc_passwd
takeaways: Autoescaping covers XSS only if you never bypass it with |safe on user data
Flask has no CSRF protection: add Flask-WTF's CSRFProtect
Secure cookie settings, MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH and hashed passwords are must-haves
pitfalls: Assuming Flask protects forms from CSRF by default.

quiz.q: Which protection does Flask itself NOT provide out of the box?
quiz.explain: CSRF protection comes from extensions like Flask-WTF; Flask itself only escapes templates and signs sessions.

concepts.name: Deploying to production
concepts.summary: Run Flask under a production WSGI server like Gunicorn behind a reverse proxy, with ProxyFix, logging and static files handled.
concepts.why: The development server isn't built for real traffic; production needs the right server, a proxy in front and safe settings.
concepts.body:
Putting your app online, **deploying** it, starts with a proper **WSGI server**: a program that speaks WSGI and runs several copies of your app, called **workers**, so many requests are handled at once:

```bash
gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 "myapp:create_app()"
```

**Gunicorn** runs on Linux and macOS; Waitress is a pure-Python option that also works on Windows. Gunicorn suggests (2 x CPU cores) + 1 workers as a starting point. If your views spend most of their time waiting (on a database or other services), add `--threads`, or use gevent workers for many slow connections.

Put a **reverse proxy** in front: a server such as Nginx or Caddy, or a load balancer from your hosting provider, that receives every request first. It handles the HTTPS encryption, waits for slow clients so your workers don't have to, sends `/static` files itself, and passes the rest on to Gunicorn.

Behind a proxy, Flask sees the proxy's address and plain HTTP, unless you trust the `X-Forwarded-*` headers in which the proxy reports the visitor's real address and scheme. Wrap the app with **ProxyFix**, saying how many proxies set each header:

```python
app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(app.wsgi_app, x_for=1, x_proto=1, x_host=1)
```

Only do this when a proxy really sets them; otherwise visitors can fake their IP address and scheme.

Checklist:

- debug mode off; `SECRET_KEY` and database passwords from the environment
- secure cookie settings and `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`
- logs: write `app.logger` messages and the server's list of requests to the terminal output, where your hosting platform collects them
- database migrations run as a separate release step, not inside `create_app`
- a **health check** route that returns "ok", which the platform calls regularly to spot a broken copy
- package the app as a small container image (a sealed bundle of the app and everything it needs) that doesn't run as the all-powerful root user

Platforms like Render, Fly.io or any cloud that runs containers all follow this same Gunicorn-plus-proxy shape.
takeaways: Use Gunicorn or Waitress, never flask run, in production
A reverse proxy handles HTTPS and static files
ProxyFix with the right counts restores the visitor's IP address and scheme behind a proxy
pitfalls: Enabling ProxyFix without a proxy in front, letting visitors fake X-Forwarded-For.

quiz.q: Behind Nginx, url_for(..., _external=True) produces http:// links although users use HTTPS. What fixes it?
options: Moving static files to a CDN
Wrapping app.wsgi_app with ProxyFix(x_proto=1) and having Nginx send X-Forwarded-Proto
quiz.explain: Flask only sees the plain-HTTP connection from the proxy; ProxyFix trusts the scheme the proxy forwards.

concepts.name: WSGI and Werkzeug under the hood
concepts.summary: See Flask as a WSGI app built on Werkzeug's routing, request and response objects, and write your own WSGI middleware.
concepts.why: Knowing the layer below Flask demystifies servers, middleware and many confusing errors.
concepts.body:
**WSGI** (defined in PEP 3333, a Python design document) is the contract between Python web servers and apps: the app is a callable `app(environ, start_response)`. `environ` is a dict describing the request with keys such as `REQUEST_METHOD`, `PATH_INFO` and `wsgi.input` (the body). The app calls `start_response(status, headers)` and returns an iterable of bytes. Gunicorn, uWSGI, Waitress and the development server all speak this contract.

A Flask object is exactly such a callable. `Flask.__call__` hands over to `app.wsgi_app`, which:

1. builds a request context from `environ` and pushes it (and the app context)
2. matches the URL using Werkzeug's routing (`app.url_map`, a `Map` of `Rule`s with converters)
3. runs `before_request` hooks, the view and `after_request` hooks
4. turns the return value into a Werkzeug `Response` with `make_response`
5. calls the response as a WSGI app, then pops the contexts and runs the teardown functions

**Werkzeug** supplies the `Request` and `Response` classes, URL matching, HTTP exceptions such as `NotFound`, the development server with its reloader and debugger, and helpers such as `secure_filename`. Flask adds the app object, contexts, blueprints, config, Jinja support and the `flask` command.

Because `wsgi_app` is separate from `__call__`, middleware wraps it: `app.wsgi_app = Middleware(app.wsgi_app)` keeps `app` itself as the Flask object, so extensions and `app.config` still work. Werkzeug's `DispatcherMiddleware` can mount several apps under different path prefixes.

WSGI is **synchronous**: a request occupies a worker thread from start to finish, until the app returns. That fact shapes how Flask handles many requests at once (its concurrency, see the last lesson), and it is why connections that stay open for a long time, such as WebSockets (two-way connections for live updates), need other tools.
takeaways: A WSGI app is app(environ, start_response) returning bytes
Flask.__call__ -> wsgi_app: contexts, routing, hooks, view, response
Wrap app.wsgi_app (not app) with middleware
Werkzeug provides routing, Request/Response and the dev server
pitfalls: Replacing app itself with middleware (app = Middleware(app)), which breaks app.config and the CLI.

quiz.q: Why does Flask recommend app.wsgi_app = Middleware(app.wsgi_app) instead of app = Middleware(app)?
options: app stays the Flask object, so config, extensions and the CLI keep working
quiz.explain: Wrapping the inner wsgi_app preserves the Flask instance while still intercepting every request.

concepts.name: How request and current_app proxies work
concepts.summary: Learn how Flask's request and current_app are LocalProxy objects reading context variables, and how to use them safely with threads.
concepts.why: Understanding the proxies explains context errors, bugs with threads, and when you need the real object.
concepts.body:
`request`, `session`, `g` and `current_app` look like module globals, yet requests handled at the same time each see their own values. In Flask 3, the active contexts are stored in **context variables** (`contextvars.ContextVar` from the standard library: variables whose value is separate for each thread and each asyncio task). The names you import are Werkzeug **`LocalProxy`** objects that look up the current value every time you use them.

Consequences:

- Each thread (and each asyncio task) has its own context-variable values, so requests handled by different threads never see each other's `request`.
- Using a proxy with no active context raises `RuntimeError`.
- A proxy is not the object itself: `isinstance(request, Request)` is `True` through the proxy, but `type(request)` is `LocalProxy`. When you need the real object, for example to hand it to another thread, call `request._get_current_object()` (or `current_app._get_current_object()`).

**New threads do not inherit the context.** A thread started from a view begins with empty context variables, so using `request` there fails. Options:

- pass plain data (IDs, dicts) into the thread, the cleanest choice
- push a context inside the thread with `with app.app_context():`, using the real app object
- decorate the function with `@copy_current_request_context`

Contexts behave like a stack: pushing an app context inside another (as with nested test clients) hides the outer one until it is popped. Always use `with` blocks so they are popped even when an error happens; otherwise leftover state leaks into later code.

The design keeps view signatures clean at the cost of hidden state: use proxies at the edges of your app (views, hooks) and pass explicit values into your core logic.
takeaways: Flask's request, session, g and current_app are LocalProxy objects reading context variables
New threads start without a context; pass data or push one
_get_current_object() returns the real object behind a proxy
pitfalls: Passing the request proxy into a background thread and reading it after the request ended.

quiz.q: A view starts a threading.Thread whose function reads request.args. What happens?
options: It works because request is global
It raises RuntimeError: no request context in the new thread
It reads the args of a random request
It blocks until the request finishes
quiz.explain: Context variables are not inherited by new threads, so the proxy finds no active request.

concepts.name: Async views and the concurrency model
concepts.summary: Know how Flask handles simultaneous requests, what async def views really do, and when to choose Quart or another framework.
concepts.why: Choosing the right kind of worker, and the right expectations of async, decides how a Flask app behaves under heavy traffic.
concepts.body:
Flask is a WSGI framework: **one request occupies one worker** (a process, thread or greenlet) from start to finish. Handling many requests at once therefore comes from the server:

- **sync workers**: N processes, N simultaneous requests; simple and robust when views do little heavy computing
- **threads** (`gunicorn --threads 8`): more requests waiting on I/O per process; your code and libraries must be thread-safe
- **gevent or eventlet workers**: thousands of **greenlets** (very light threads run by a library), made possible by quietly replacing the standard library's network functions with cooperative versions. Good for many slow connections, but every library you use must play along.

**`async def` views** are supported since Flask 2.0 after `pip install "flask[async]"` (which installs asgiref). Each async view runs in an event loop on the worker thread handling the request. Inside one view you can `await asyncio.gather(...)` to run several I/O calls at the same time, which is the real benefit. But the worker stays busy until the view finishes, so async views do **not** let one worker serve more requests at once, and they add a little extra cost.

Things that don't fit this one-request-per-worker design: WebSockets, server-sent events (a response that stays open and keeps pushing updates) to many clients, and long polling (holding requests open until there is news) at scale. Use **Quart** (Flask's API rebuilt on **ASGI**, the async successor of WSGI), FastAPI or Starlette for those, or a separate service.

Background work (emails, reports) shouldn't run inside the request at all: hand it to a **task queue** (a list of jobs that separate worker processes pick up) such as Celery or RQ, or a small thread pool for simple cases, and return immediately.

Measure before changing anything: most Flask apps are limited by the database, so the number of database connections and queries matters more than the kind of worker.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, time
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)       # requires: pip install "flask[async]"

async def fetch(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)            # stands in for an HTTP or DB call
    return name

@app.get("/dashboard")
async def dashboard():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    users, orders, stats = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("users", 0.2), fetch("orders", 0.2), fetch("stats", 0.2))
    return {"parts": [users, orders, stats],
            "took_s": round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1)}

print(app.test_client().get("/dashboard").json)
# {'parts': ['users', 'orders', 'stats'], 'took_s': 0.2}   (not 0.6)
takeaways: Each request holds a worker until it finishes; concurrency comes from workers, threads or greenlets
async views let several awaits run at once inside one request
Use Quart/FastAPI for WebSockets and huge numbers of open connections; use task queues for background work
pitfalls: Converting views to async def expecting each worker to handle more requests.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of an async def view in Flask?
options: One worker can serve many requests at once
Several awaited I/O calls within one request can run concurrently
It removes the need for a WSGI server
quiz.explain: The view still occupies its worker; the gain is that awaits inside that one request run at the same time.
